author: Ryan Archer
title: A Little Vodka Made German Speakers' Dutch Sound Better to Native Ears, but the Speakers Couldn't Tell
text:
A Little Vodka Made German Speakers' Dutch Sound Better to Native Ears, but the Speakers Couldn't Tell
People often joke that a drink loosens the tongue in a foreign language. A small experiment found that native listeners agreed, at least about how the speakers sounded. The speakers themselves noticed no difference.
In the study, 50 native German speakers who had recently learned Dutch were randomly assigned to drink a small dose of alcohol or water before chatting in Dutch. Two native Dutch speakers who did not know who had been drinking rated the alcohol group's Dutch better overall. The work, published in the Journal of Psychopharmacology, won the 2025 Ig Nobel Peace Prize.
A Small Drink and a Two-Minute Conversation
The researchers were Fritz Renner, Inge Kersbergen, Matt Field, and Jessica Werthmann, who at the time were affiliated with Maastricht University, the University of Liverpool, King's College London, and other institutions. The paper appeared online in October 2017 and in print in January 2018.
Participants were psychology students at Maastricht University who had passed a Dutch proficiency exam. The researchers had expected alcohol to make their Dutch worse, since it impairs memory and attention.
The alcohol group drank vodka mixed with bitter lemon, with the amount set by body weight and sex to reach a low target breath alcohol level of about 0.04%. The University of Liverpool's announcement of the study compared the dose to just under a pint of 5% beer for a 70-kilogram man. The control group drank water.
Each participant then held a brief, standardized discussion in Dutch about animal testing with an experimenter who did not know which drink they had received. The conversations were recorded so native Dutch speakers could rate them later without knowing group assignments. Participants also rated their own Dutch.
Listeners Heard Better Dutch, Speakers Felt No Change
The observers rated the alcohol group's Dutch significantly better overall. In an exploratory analysis, the difference appeared to come mainly from pronunciation. Grammar, vocabulary, and argumentation did not differ significantly between groups.
Alcohol did not affect how participants rated their own skills. That gap is the most intriguing part of the result. If alcohol had simply made people feel more confident, they might have rated themselves higher. Instead, the change showed up only to outside listeners.
"This provides some support for the lay belief (among bilingual speakers) that a low dose of alcohol can improve their ability to speak a second language," Kersbergen said when the study was released.
The researchers were careful about why it happened. "We need to be cautious about the implications of these results until we know more about what causes the observed results," Werthmann said. She suggested that alcohol's anxiety-reducing effect could be one explanation, though the study did not measure anxiety.
"It is important to point out that participants in this study consumed a low dose of alcohol," Renner said. "Higher levels of alcohol consumption might not have beneficial effects on the pronunciation of a foreign language."
The Researchers Do Not Recommend Drinking to Speak Better
The team received the 2025 Ig Nobel Peace Prize in September 2025, honored, in the organizers' words, for showing that drinking alcohol sometimes improves a person's ability to speak a foreign language, according to Improbable Research. Renner and Werthmann, now at the University of Freiburg in Germany, accepted on the team's behalf at the ceremony in Boston.
The University of Bath, where Kersbergen now works, stressed that the findings do not encourage drinking. "I would not recommend that anyone uses alcohol to improve their fluency in a second language," Kersbergen said.
Alcohol carries broader risks. The National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism says harms may be associated with any amount of drinking, and that even one drink a day can raise a woman's breast cancer risk by 5% to 15% compared with not drinking. The agency advises avoiding alcohol entirely before driving or operating machinery, when taking medications that interact with it, during pregnancy or when pregnancy is possible, and for anyone under 21.
Small Study, Narrow Findings
The experiment was small and brief. It used a convenience sample without a formal power calculation, tested one low dose and one short conversation, and involved one closely related language pair. German and Dutch share a great deal, so the results may not apply to learners of very different languages.
Because the control group drank water, the study cannot separate the effect of alcohol itself from participants' expectations of being drunk. It also did not use professional language assessments, and it measured how speech sounded, not comprehension or long-term learning. Higher doses could easily worsen performance.
For language learners, the more useful takeaway may be about nerves rather than drinks. If anxiety holds back pronunciation, practicing in low-pressure settings could be a safer way to test the idea, though the study did not examine that.
People who are concerned about their drinking can find help through the NIAAA's Alcohol Treatment Navigator or by talking with a health care professional.
Key Questions Answered
What did the Dutch courage study test?
Whether a low dose of alcohol changed how well 50 German speakers who had recently learned Dutch spoke during a short conversation.
What did researchers find?
Native Dutch listeners rated the alcohol group's Dutch better overall, mainly in pronunciation. The speakers' own ratings did not change.
How much alcohol did participants drink?
A small, weight-adjusted amount of vodka aimed at a breath alcohol level of about 0.04%, which the university compared to just under a pint of 5% beer for a 70-kilogram man.
Why might a small drink help pronunciation?
The authors suggested reduced anxiety, but they did not measure it, so the reason remains unknown.
Do the researchers recommend drinking before speaking a foreign language?
No. Co-author Inge Kersbergen said she would not recommend using alcohol to improve fluency, and higher doses impair thinking and motor skills.
Does this apply to other languages?
Unknown. The study involved one closely related language pair, one low dose, and one brief conversation.
